title: How tangent vectors and covectors change with coordinates
summary: The transformation law for the components of a tangent vector and a covector, why the two laws are inverse to each other, and how that makes g_ij dx^i dx^j a coordinate-free object.

check.prompt: On ℝ² \ {0}, the vector field ∂/∂r of polar coordinates is written in Cartesian components. Find its components (vˣ, vʸ) at the point with polar coordinates (r, θ), and check them against the transformation law.
check.guidance: With x = r cos θ, y = r sin θ, the law v'^i = (∂x^i/∂u^j) v^j applied to the polar components (v^r, v^θ) = (1, 0) gives vˣ = ∂x/∂r = cos θ and vʸ = ∂y/∂r = sin θ. So ∂/∂r = cos θ ∂/∂x + sin θ ∂/∂y = (x/r) ∂/∂x + (y/r) ∂/∂y: the unit radial field, as the picture suggests. Note that ∂/∂θ = −r sin θ ∂/∂x + r cos θ ∂/∂y has length r, not 1: coordinate vector fields need not be unit vectors.

sources.note: Tangent vectors defined as equivalence classes of chart–vector pairs, related by the derivative of the transition map: the law stated here.

checks.name: mathematical-review
checks.evidence: Author's own review: the vector law v'^i = (∂x'^i/∂x^j) v^j follows from the chain rule on a curve; the covector law ω'_i = (∂x^j/∂x'^i) ω_j follows from ω(v) being chart-independent; their Jacobians are mutually inverse; the metric components transform with two inverse Jacobians so g_ij dx^i dx^j is invariant; the polar example g = dr² + r² dθ² recomputed from dx = cos θ dr − r sin θ dθ, dy = sin θ dr + r cos θ dθ; the check's ∂/∂r = cos θ ∂x + sin θ ∂y.

checks.name: consistency-with-course
checks.evidence: Matches MAT-262 unit 1's coordinate expressions of a metric and its distinction between a coordinate singularity and a property of the metric (the polar metric's det = r² vanishing at r = 0).
